lines: Before you can budget, save or invest, your money needs a home. For most people, that home is a bank, and it comes with two kinds of accounts.
The first is a checking account. Think of it as your wallet. Your paycheck lands there, your debit card pulls from it, and your bills come out of it.
The second is a savings account. Think of it as a jar on a high shelf. It's for money you don't need this month, and the bank pays you interest to keep it there.
Banks show that interest as an APY, the percent your money earns in a year. At four percent, five hundred dollars earns about twenty dollars a year, without you doing anything.
Most checking accounts pay little or nothing. So extra money sitting in checking is money that could be earning, but isn't.
But you can't put everything in savings, either. Your card and your bills pull from checking, and many banks limit how often you can take money out of savings.
If checking runs dry and the bank covers a purchase anyway, that's an overdraft. Some banks charge about thirty-five dollars for it, even if you were only a few dollars short.
So here's the simple rule. Keep enough in checking for your spending until the next paycheck, plus a cushion for surprises. Move the rest to savings.
With nine hundred dollars and two hundred fifty in bills, that could be four hundred in checking and five hundred in savings.
Checking is for spending. Savings is for waiting. Give each dollar the right home, and everything else in this course gets easier.
